title: Can You Voluntarily Stop Your Pulse? The Science Behind Heart Rate and the Arterial Pulse

html:
Introduction

The pulse is a palpable pressure wave that travels through the arterial system following ventricular contraction and ejection of blood from the heart. Each effective cardiac contraction generates a pressure wave that propagates through the arterial walls and can be detected at peripheral sites such as the radial or carotid arteries.

Although pulse rate and heart rate are commonly used interchangeably, they are not always identical. Heart rate refers to the number of cardiac contractions per minute, whereas pulse rate refers to the number of detectable arterial pulse waves. Under certain circumstances, some cardiac contractions may fail to generate a sufficiently strong peripheral pulse wave, producing a pulse deficit. ScienceDirect – Pulse Rate⁠￼

How Is the Heartbeat Generated?

The heartbeat originates from the heart’s intrinsic electrical conduction system. Under normal conditions, the sinoatrial (SA) node generates spontaneous electrical impulses that spread through the atria and subsequently pass through the atrioventricular node and ventricular conduction system. This coordinated electrical activation produces rhythmic contraction of the cardiac chambers.

The autonomic nervous system continuously modifies cardiac activity. Sympathetic stimulation can increase heart rate and contractility, while parasympathetic activity, predominantly through the vagus nerve, can slow the heart rate. However, these regulatory mechanisms do not mean that the heartbeat is under direct voluntary control.

Can You Voluntarily Stop Your Pulse?

Normally, no.

The pulse is a downstream consequence of ventricular contraction and the generation of arterial pressure. Because the heart possesses an intrinsic pacemaking and conduction system, a person cannot simply decide to switch off the heart or deliberately eliminate the arterial pulse through ordinary voluntary actions.

Certain activities can temporarily influence heart rate. For example, changes in breathing, emotional state, physical activity, posture, or autonomic nervous system activity may cause the heart rate to increase or decrease. However, these effects represent indirect modulation, rather than conscious control over whether the heart beats.

Why Might Someone Think Their Pulse Has Disappeared?

A pulse can sometimes become difficult to detect without the heart actually stopping.

The strength of a peripheral pulse depends on several factors, including cardiac output, arterial pressure, vascular resistance and the characteristics of the arterial pulse wave. A weak cardiac contraction may therefore produce a pulse wave that is difficult to palpate at a peripheral site.

This is also why heart rate and pulse rate can occasionally differ. When some cardiac contractions fail to generate detectable peripheral pulse waves, a pulse deficit occurs. ScienceDirect – Pulse Rate⁠￼

Therefore, not being able to feel a pulse at one particular location does not necessarily mean that the heart has stopped. Clinical assessment should use appropriate methods rather than relying solely on palpation of a peripheral pulse.

Can Breathing Techniques Stop the Heart?

Breathing techniques can influence autonomic nervous system activity and consequently alter heart rate. Slow breathing, for example, can enhance vagal influences on the heart and produce changes in beat-to-beat heart rate.

However, this is fundamentally different from voluntarily stopping the heart.

The intrinsic electrical activity of the heart continues independently of conscious intention. Extreme physiological disturbances can cause dangerous cardiac rhythm abnormalities, but deliberately attempting to produce such a state is neither a normal physiological phenomenon nor a safe practice.

What Happens When the Heart Actually Stops?

If the heart suddenly ceases to generate effective mechanical contractions, effective circulation stops, and the body is no longer adequately supplied with oxygenated blood. This produces cardiac arrest, which is a medical emergency requiring immediate resuscitation.

This is fundamentally different from temporarily slowing the heart through normal autonomic regulation.

Conclusion

The pulse is the arterial pressure wave generated by effective cardiac contraction. Although people can influence heart rate indirectly through autonomic mechanisms, they cannot normally exert direct voluntary control over the heart’s intrinsic rhythm or intentionally switch off their pulse.

Furthermore, heart rate and pulse rate are not always identical because some cardiac contractions may fail to produce a detectable peripheral pulse wave, resulting in a pulse deficit. ScienceDirect – Pulse Rate⁠￼

The ability to influence heart rate is therefore not the same as the ability to voluntarily stop the heartbeat.
